0.title: Truth and Grace for Broken Covenants
0.essay:
Divorce touches almost every family and every church. Few subjects call more urgently for both faithfulness to Scripture and deep compassion.

Who this is for

Some readers have been divorced. Some are in painful marriages and wonder whether they may leave. Some have remarried and wonder whether they did wrong. Some are children of divorce, still feeling its effects years later. And many churches struggle to know how to apply Scripture with both faithfulness and kindness.

What Scripture does

The Bible speaks clearly about God’s design for marriage and his hatred of covenant-breaking. It also speaks honestly about a world where marriages are broken by sin, and it gives limited permission for divorce in certain situations. Christians have disagreed about the details, so this study sets out the main views before giving a verdict.

Above all, grace

Above all, the gospel speaks to this subject with grace. Jesus spoke tenderly to a woman who had had five husbands (John 4). No divorce is beyond God’s forgiveness, and no divorced person is a second-class Christian. The church must hold God’s standard high and its arms wide open.

The chapters

God’s Design and the Pain of Divorce; Why Moses Permitted Divorce; Grounds for Divorce; Abuse, Separation and Hard Cases; and Remarriage and Grace. The Christian Marriage study covers building strong marriages.

For reflection

How has divorce touched your own life or family? Bring that to God honestly as you begin.

1.title: God's Design and the Pain of Divorce
1.essay:
Every discussion of divorce must begin where Jesus began: not with exceptions, but with God’s design for marriage.

One flesh

Marriage was God’s idea. When he brought the woman to the man, Adam rejoiced, and Scripture gives the definition of marriage: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Marriage is a covenant, a solemn promise before God, joining husband and wife in a lifelong union of body, life and love.

What God has joined

When the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with a question about divorce, he went straight back to creation and concluded, “So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6). Marriage is not merely a human contract to be ended when feelings change. God himself joins husband and wife.

A contract can be ended when one party fails to deliver. A covenant is a binding promise made before witnesses and before God. The traditional vow, “till death us do part,” reflects this.

God hates covenant-breaking

In Malachi’s day, men in Judah were divorcing their wives to marry younger foreign women. They still brought offerings to the temple, and wept when God did not accept them. God told them why: “the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).

He went on: “For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence” (Malachi 2:16). Unjust divorce is a kind of violence against a spouse. And God added, “So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless” (Malachi 2:16). He was not interested in worship from men who betrayed their wives.

A picture of Christ

Paul says marriage is a picture of Christ’s covenant love for his church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Husbands are to love their wives “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Christ never abandons his bride. That is why faithfulness in marriage matters so much: it proclaims his faithfulness.

The pain of divorce

Divorce tears apart what God joined, and the tearing hurts. Spouses, children, extended families and churches all suffer. Even when divorce is permitted, it is always the result of sin somewhere, and it is always a tragedy. It should be the last resort, never the first.

Reconciliation first

Because of God’s design, the first goal in a troubled marriage should always be repentance, forgiveness and reconciliation. The Forgiveness and Reconciliation study explores this further.

Think of a couple whose marriage has grown cold. Both are quietly thinking about divorce. Before deciding anything, they agree to see a Christian counsellor and to read Matthew 19 together. It is hard work: months of honesty and repentance. Two years later their marriage is not perfect, but it is alive, and they are glad they did not give up.

Grace for the divorced

To say God hates divorce is not to say God hates divorced people. Many divorced people were sinned against, sometimes terribly. And all of us, like every sinner, are welcome at the cross. A church can uphold God’s design without condemning those whose marriages have broken. In fact, it must do both.

For reflection

If you are married, are you building your marriage on covenant commitment or on feelings? How can your church uphold God’s design while welcoming those whose marriages have ended?

2.title: Why Moses Permitted Divorce
2.essay:
If God hates divorce, why did the law of Moses allow it? Jesus’ answer tells us a great deal about God’s patience with a sinful world, and about the seriousness of marriage.

The law of Moses

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 assumed that divorce happened in Israel and regulated it. If a man divorced his wife “because he has found some indecency in her” (Deuteronomy 24:1), he had to give her a written certificate of divorce. If she then married another man and that marriage ended, the first husband could not take her back.

The law did not command divorce. It limited its damage. In the ancient world, a woman sent away without a certificate could not remarry and might be left destitute. The certificate protected her and freed her to marry again. The rule against remarrying the first husband also discouraged hasty divorce. God’s law cared for the vulnerable even while regulating sin.

Because of hardness of heart

The Pharisees thought Moses had commanded divorce. They asked Jesus, “Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?” (Matthew 19:7). Jesus corrected them: “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8).

Divorce was a concession to human sin, not part of God’s original design. And the root of divorce is still hardness of heart: a refusal to forgive, repent or keep promises. The gospel softens hearts, which is why Christians should be slow to divorce.

The debate in Jesus’ day

Jewish teachers disagreed about Deuteronomy 24. Some held that a man could divorce his wife for almost any reason, even burning a meal. Others limited it to serious sexual sin. So the Pharisees’ question, “Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?” (Matthew 19:3), was a trap set in the middle of a live debate. Jesus refused to be drawn into their categories, and went back to creation.

God’s own divorce

Strikingly, God himself speaks of divorcing faithless Israel because of her persistent spiritual adultery with idols. “I had sent her away with a decree of divorce” (Jeremiah 3:8). This shows that divorce is not always sinful for the innocent party. God was the wronged husband.

Yet even then, God called his people back: “Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful” (Jeremiah 3:12). The divine husband who was wronged still longed for reconciliation.

Hosea lived this out. His wife Gomer was repeatedly unfaithful. Yet God told Hosea to buy her back and love her, “even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (Hosea 3:1). Hosea’s marriage became a living picture of God’s relentless love.

Jesus raised the standard

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus quoted the common understanding of the law and sharpened it: “But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (Matthew 5:32). He rejected easy divorce and restored the seriousness of the marriage covenant against a culture that treated it lightly.

Permission, not command

Moses permitted divorce; he did not command it. Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality; he does not require it. Forgiveness and reconciliation remain the better path wherever possible.

Think of a woman who discovers her husband has been having an affair. She has biblical grounds for divorce. But he repents deeply, ends the affair and seeks counselling. With much pain and prayer, she chooses to forgive and rebuild. She knows she was not required to. She believes God helped her. It takes years, but their marriage is restored.

That is not to say every wronged spouse must do the same. The permission is real, and those who use it are not sinning. But it is a permission given with sorrow, as a concession to sin, not a right to be claimed eagerly.

For reflection

Do you see divorce as a right, or as a sad concession to sin? What does God’s call to faithless Israel, “Return,” teach you about his heart?

3.title: Grounds for Divorce
3.essay:
Does Scripture permit divorce at all? If so, when? This is where Christians differ most, and where clear thinking matters most for real people in real pain.

Sexual immorality

Jesus said, “And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery” (Matthew 19:9). His exception shows that sexual unfaithfulness so breaks the one-flesh union that the innocent spouse may end the marriage. This permission is not a requirement. The wronged spouse may forgive and stay.

Jesus’ teaching was so strict that his disciples said, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry” (Matthew 19:10). He then spoke of those who remain single for the kingdom. Marriage is serious; singleness is honourable.

What about Mark and Luke?

Mark and Luke record Jesus’ teaching without the exception (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18). Many explain this by noting that their readers would have assumed adultery ended a marriage, as both Jewish and Roman law already did. Matthew, writing for a Jewish audience caught up in the debate over Deuteronomy 24, makes the exception explicit. The Gospels do not contradict each other. Matthew states what the others assume.

Desertion by an unbeliever

Paul addresses a situation Jesus did not: a believer married to an unbeliever. In Corinth, some new Christians wondered whether they should leave their unbelieving spouses. Paul told them to stay if the spouse was willing, because the believer’s presence was a blessing to the home: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:16).

But if the unbeliever leaves, things are different: “But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace” (1 Corinthians 7:15). When an unbelieving spouse abandons the marriage, the believer is not bound.

Separation without grounds

For believers married to believers, Paul passes on the Lord’s own command: “the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:10–11). Separation is not a loophole for remarriage. Those who separate without biblical grounds should seek reconciliation.

What is not a ground

Incompatibility, unhappiness, falling out of love, boredom, or finding someone else are not biblical grounds for divorce. These are reasons to seek help, to repent and to rebuild. Many marriages pass through long seasons where these feelings are strong, and come out the other side.

The views

Some Christians hold that divorce is never permitted, reading Mark 10:11–12 and Luke 16:18, which have no exception. Others hold that adultery is the only ground. Others, following the historic Protestant confessions, permit divorce for adultery and for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied. Some go further and allow divorce for many reasons.

The verdict

The confessional view is the most faithful. Matthew records Jesus’ exception for sexual immorality, which Mark and Luke assume rather than state. Paul adds desertion by an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:15). And many Reformed churches apply that principle to a professing believer who deserts and refuses all correction, who is then to be treated “as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17). Outside these grounds, believers should not divorce.

Not alone

Decisions about divorce should never be made alone. Elders and wise counsellors should be involved, to seek reconciliation, to discern the situation and to protect the vulnerable.

Think of a man whose wife leaves him and their children, moves in with another man, and refuses all contact with the church. The elders try for many months to call her to repentance. Eventually, after she files for divorce, they counsel him that he is free. He grieves deeply. But he is not condemned, and he has not walked the road alone.

For reflection

If someone asked you what Scripture says about grounds for divorce, could you explain Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:15? Why does it matter that such decisions involve the church?

4.title: Abuse, Separation and Hard Cases
4.essay:
Some of the most painful situations involve abuse: physical violence, sexual abuse, threats, or severe and controlling emotional cruelty. What does Scripture say to a spouse living with abuse?

Safety first

Paul’s instruction that a wife should not separate from her husband (1 Corinthians 7:10) does not require anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. Leaving to be safe is not the separation Paul forbids.

Scripture repeatedly commends fleeing from danger. When Saul, in a jealous rage, threw a spear at David and then sent men to kill him, Michal helped him escape: “So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped” (1 Samuel 19:12). David fled even though Saul was the anointed king, and Scripture does not condemn him. Jesus told his followers, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” (Matthew 10:23). And Proverbs says, “The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3).

A spouse or parent who seeks safety from violence is acting wisely, not faithlessly. A church must never send a victim back to an abuser.

Abuse is a crime

Abuse is a crime as well as a sin. It should be reported to the authorities. The governing authority “is God’s servant for your good,” and “he does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). Reporting abuse is not revenge or betrayal. It is using the protection God has provided. The abuser should also face the church’s discipline. Church and state each have a role in restraining evil.

Headship is not tyranny

Scripture calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church. Paul adds, “For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church” (Ephesians 5:29). Christ’s headship is self-sacrificing love, never cruelty. A husband who abuses his wife is not exercising headship; he is betraying it, and betraying the gospel picture of marriage. Complementarian teaching must never be used to excuse abuse.

Does abuse end the marriage?

Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse ends the marriage itself is a harder question. Malachi links faithlessness and violence: the man who divorces his wife without love “covers his garment with violence” (Malachi 2:16). Abuse breaks the covenant at its heart.

Many Reformed pastors and church courts treat persistent, unrepentant abuse as a form of the desertion Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 7:15. The abuser has abandoned every promise of the marriage while remaining under the same roof. A spouse who has been driven out by violence has, in truth, been deserted.

Repentance and trust

An abuser who claims repentance must show it over time. True repentance accepts consequences, seeks help, submits to accountability, and does not demand that the victim return. Forgiveness can be given, but trust must be rebuilt slowly, and safety must always come first.

How a church should respond

Churches must take reports of abuse seriously, protect victims, involve the authorities, and never put keeping a marriage together above the safety of its members.

Think of a woman who finally tells her pastor that her husband has hit her for years. The pastor believes her. He helps her find a safe place to stay with her children, encourages her to contact the police, and confronts the husband together with the elders. The church supports her practically and spiritually. When the husband refuses to repent, the elders counsel her that she is not bound.

Other hard cases

Some situations are complicated in other ways: addiction, mental illness, a spouse who is a Christian in name only, financial abandonment. These need wise, patient pastoral care, honest assessment and prayer. Every case is different, and each person needs to be cared for individually, not handled with a formula.

For reflection

Does your church know how to respond to abuse? If someone confided in you, what would you do first? Why is it wrong to use biblical teaching on marriage to keep anyone in danger?

5.title: Remarriage and Grace
5.essay:
After a marriage has ended, many ask: may I marry again? And those who already have remarried often ask: did I do wrong, and what should I do now?

The innocent party

Where a marriage has been broken by a spouse’s adultery, Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:9 imply that the innocent partner who remarries does not commit adultery. Where a believer has been deserted, Paul says the believer “is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). The historic Protestant confessions conclude that remarriage is then permitted, as if the offending party were dead.

When remarriage is not permitted

Paul’s instruction to “remain unmarried or else be reconciled” (1 Corinthians 7:11) is given to someone who has separated without grounds. Those who divorce without biblical grounds should seek reconciliation, not a new marriage.

Widows and widowers

Death ends a marriage. “A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Paul thinks she may be happier single, but marriage is permitted, and a believer must marry a believer. Paul uses the same principle as an illustration in Romans 7:2–3. He is not giving a full treatment of divorce there, but the illustration shows how seriously he takes the marriage bond.

The views

Some Christians hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives, pointing to Romans 7:2–3, 1 Corinthians 7:39 and Mark 10:11–12. Others hold that the innocent party in a divorce for adultery or desertion may remarry. Some allow remarriage more broadly.

The verdict

The innocent party in a biblically justified divorce may remarry. Jesus’ exception in Matthew 19:9 governs both the divorce and the remarriage that follows. Being “not enslaved” means free from the marriage bond. Romans 7 and 1 Corinthians 7:39 describe the normal rule for an intact marriage, not the situation after adultery or desertion.

Those already remarried

Many Christians remarried before coming to faith, or without understanding Scripture, or in situations that were not clear. They are not to break up the marriage they are in. They are to repent of any sin in how it began and keep the vows they have now made. A second divorce would not undo the first. It would only add another broken covenant.

Think of a man who divorced his first wife years ago, before he was a Christian, for no good reason. He has since remarried. After coming to faith, he is troubled by Matthew 19:9. His pastor helps him see that he should not leave his present wife. Instead he should repent before God, seek his first wife’s forgiveness if that is possible, and be faithful to the marriage he is in. He finds peace.

Grace at the well

Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well and told her, “you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18). He did not ignore her situation. But he did not shame her either. He offered her living water and revealed himself as the Messiah. She ran back to her town saying, “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29). Truth spoken in grace led to her salvation, and to many others’.

No divorce is beyond the reach of Christ’s forgiveness. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). This truth reaches the divorced and remarried as fully as anyone. Rahab, a former prostitute, and Ruth, a Moabite widow, are both named in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). God weaves broken stories into his redemption.

Church leadership

Whether a divorced or remarried man may serve as an elder is debated. “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2) most naturally means a man who is faithful to his wife. Elders must weigh the circumstances and the man’s present reputation, not simply his history.

The church’s welcome

Divorced people should be fully welcomed in the church: cared for, included and loved. Their children need special care. Single parents need practical support with meals, lifts, childcare and simple friendship. The church is meant to be a family for those whose families have been broken.

For reflection

How does your church treat divorced and remarried people? Is it a place of both truth and grace? What could you do to care for a single parent or a child of divorce this month?
